commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Fill in programming and IDE experience
Chatbot: Rename to Rocky, add greet and exit
Echo user input, exit on bye command
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously the chatbot only greeted the user and exited immediately,
without reading any input.

Let's add a loop that reads each line of user input and echoes it
back, until the user types "bye", at which point the chatbot prints
the farewell message and exits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add task storage and list command
Chatbot: Add mark and unmark task commands
Add support for ToDos, Deadlines, and Events
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously all user input was stored as a plain string, so the app
could not distinguish between task kinds or attach date/time info.

Add a Task class hierarchy so each task kind owns its own display
logic:

* Task: abstract base holding the description and done status
* Todo: task with no date/time attached
* Deadline: task with a /by date/time
* Event: task with /from and /to date/times

Add a TaskType enum that pairs each kind's command keyword with its
list icon (T, D, E), used for both command dispatch and rendering.

Tasks are now shown as [<type>][<status>] description, with Deadline
and Event appending their date fragment via super.toString(). Adding
a task reports the task and the updated task count.

Dates/times are stored as plain strings; parsing them into real date
objects is left for a later increment.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add assertions to document assumptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, several internal assumptions (e.g. a parsed index being
within bounds, a task list never being null, a command word always
being non-empty after splitting) were relied on implicitly, with no
way to catch a violation early if the assumption ever broke.

Let's add Java assert statements at key points across the codebase
to document and check these assumptions, such as: task indices being
within range after parseIndex, the tasks list/count never going
negative, and non-null task objects before printing. Each assertion
is intended to catch programmer errors during development/testing,
not to replace normal exception-based error handling for user input.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Replace magic command-word strings with named constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, the command words ("bye", "list", "mark", "unmark",
"delete", "find") were written as bare string literals, and some were
repeated: "bye" was checked separately in getResponse() and
isExitCommand(), and "find" appeared three times in findTasks(). A
typo in any one copy would silently break that command, and renaming
a command meant hunting down every copy.

Let's give each command word a named constant, following the "avoid
magic literals" guideline, and have getResponse() reuse
isExitCommand() so the exit command is defined in exactly one place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Extract helper for the text after a command word
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, findTasks() and addTask() each extracted the text after
their command word with the same copy-pasted expression:

    input.length() > word.length() ? input.substring(word.length()).trim() : ""

Duplicated logic has to be fixed in every copy if it ever changes, and
the ternary made a simple idea look more complicated than it is.

Let's extract getTextAfterCommand(), following the "minimize code
duplication" and "avoid complicated expressions" guidelines. The
ternary guard isn't needed: substring() at the end of a string already
returns "", so the helper is a single line. The assertion that a line
begins with its command word moves into the helper as well, so it is
stated once rather than in each caller.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Use guard clauses for task-number errors in parseIndex()
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, parseIndex() reported an out-of-range task number with a
single throw whose message was a multi-line ternary choosing between
two different errors (empty list vs. number too large). Readers had
to untangle the ternary to see that there were two separate failure
cases. It also recomputed parts[1].trim() three times.

Let's check each unusual case with its own guard clause that throws
early, following the "avoid complicated expressions" and "make the
happy path prominent" guidelines, and read the number once into a
well-named variable using getTextAfterCommand(). The messages shown
to the user are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Extract shared formatter for numbered task lists
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, listTasks() and findTasks() each built their reply with an
identical copy-pasted loop that numbered the tasks from 1, one per
line. Any change to how a list looks would have to be made twice, and
the two copies could drift apart.

Let's extract formatTaskList(heading, tasks), following the "minimize
code duplication" guideline, so each command only says what it shows
while the way a list is displayed is defined once. The output is
unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Split addTask() into smaller parsing methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, addTask() was about 55 lines long, well over the ~30-line
limit the code quality guidelines suggest. It mixed high-level steps
(create a task, add it, save, reply) with low-level string splitting
on " /by ", " /from " and " /to ", so a reader had to wade through
parsing details to see what the method does overall.

Let's move the deadline and event parsing into parseDeadline() and
parseEvent(), following the "avoid long methods" and "SLAP hard"
guidelines. addTask() now reads at a single level of abstraction:
pick the parser for the task type, then add, save, and reply. Error
messages and behavior are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Reject malformed save-file lines instead of guessing or crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, lineToTask() took two unsafe shortcuts. Its switch used
the default branch to treat any unrecognized type letter as a todo,
so a corrupted line such as "X | 0 | foo" was silently loaded as the
wrong kind of task. It also indexed the split fields directly, so a
line with missing fields (e.g. "D | 0 | return book") threw an
uncaught ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException that crashed Rocky on startup,
even though load() is designed to skip unreadable lines with a
warning.

Let's give todos their own "T" case and make the default branch
reject unknown types, following the "use the default branch"
guideline so the unexpected case is handled explicitly. Fields are now
read through getField(), which throws a RockyException when a field
is missing, so load() skips the bad line with its usual warning and
carries on loading the rest of the file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Use TaskType's icons in the save file
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, the save file's type letters "T", "D" and "E" were
hardcoded as string literals in both taskToLine() and lineToTask(),
even though TaskType already defines the same letters through
getIcon(), which nothing called. The letters were duplicated, and
TaskType's icons were effectively dead code that could silently
disagree with what was actually written to disk.

Let's write each task's letter using TaskType.getIcon(), and read it
back with a new TaskType.fromIcon() lookup that mirrors fromKeyword(),
following the "avoid magic literals" and "minimize code duplication"
guidelines. lineToTask() now switches over TaskType values, and an
unknown letter is still rejected. The save-file format itself is
unchanged, so existing saved tasks still load.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Store a task's done state as a plain boolean
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, Task stored its done state in a Boolean object and took it
as a constructor parameter, yet every subclass passed false. The
object type allowed a null that a primitive boolean cannot hold (an
assertion had to guard against it, because isDone() would throw a
NullPointerException when unboxing it), and the always-false parameter
made readers wonder when a task could ever start out done.

Let's use a primitive boolean that starts as false and drop the
parameter, following the "make the code obvious" and "KISS"
guidelines, and the "do not trip up the reader" advice against
parameters that serve no purpose. The null assertion is removed
because a primitive can never be null.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Format all task types consistently
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, the three task types printed themselves slightly
differently: a todo had a space after its type icon ("[T] [ ] read
book") while deadlines and events did not ("[D][ ] ..."), and a
deadline had no space before its date ("return book(by: Dec 01 2019)")
while an event did ("meeting (from: ...)"). Similar things that look
different for no reason trip up the reader, both of the code and of
Rocky's replies.

Let's give every type the same "[X][ ] description (details)" layout,
following the "do not trip up the reader" guideline. Only the
displayed text changes; the save-file format is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Explain why Launcher exists and update stale comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Previously, Launcher's only comment was "A launcher class to
workaround classpath issues", which doesn't say what the issue is, so
the class looks like removable boilerplate. Its public main() also had
no header comment. RockyException's comment still said its messages
are shown "via System.out", which stopped being accurate once the GUI
started showing them in dialog boxes.

Let's state the actual reason for Launcher (Java refuses to start an
Application subclass directly from a JAR that bundles JavaFX), and
describe RockyException's messages as shown by whichever UI is in use,
following the "explain WHAT and WHY, not HOW" and "write to the
reader" guidelines.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add Expense class for recorded spending
commitResults.messageBody:
Rocky can only keep track of tasks. Users also want to keep track of
what they spend money on, e.g. food, books, and transport, but there is
nothing that can represent an expense.

Let's add an Expense class that holds a description, an amount, a
category, and the date the money was spent. It also provides parsers
that validate an amount, a category, and a date given as text, so the
upcoming expense command and the expense save file can share one set
of validation rules instead of each checking input in its own way.

Amounts are stored as BigDecimal rather than double, because binary
floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly (e.g.
0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), which would show up as stray cents.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add ExpenseList to store and save expenses
commitResults.messageBody:
An Expense can now represent a single expense, but there is nowhere to
keep the expenses a user records, and they would be lost whenever Rocky
closes.

Let's add an ExpenseList that holds the recorded expenses, saves them
to their own file, data/expenses.txt, after every change, and loads
them back on startup. As with the task save file, a line that can't be
read is skipped with a warning instead of stopping the rest of the file
from loading.

Keeping expenses in their own class and file, rather than mixing them
into Rocky's task list, leaves the task commands, the task count, and
the existing task save file unaffected by this feature.

ExpenseList is an object rather than a set of static members like
Rocky, so each instance can be pointed at its own save file, e.g. a
temporary file when testing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Generalize list helpers beyond tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
parseIndex(), describeCount(), and formatTaskList() only work for the
task list: they read the task list's size directly and hard-code the
word "task" in their messages. The upcoming expense commands need the
same behavior for the expense list, e.g. to validate
"delete-expense 2" and to number the expenses in a reply.

Copying these helpers for expenses would duplicate their logic, so any
later fix would have to be made in two places.

Let's have each helper take what it needs as parameters instead: the
list's size and the words to use in messages for parseIndex() and
describeCount(), and a list of any kind of item for
formatNumberedList(), renamed from formatTaskList() as it is no longer
specific to tasks. The replies to task commands are unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add commands to record, list, and delete expenses
commitResults.messageBody:
Expense and ExpenseList can represent and save expenses, but a user
still has no way to record one.

Let's add three commands:

* expense <description> /amount <amount> /category <category>
  [/on <yyyy-mm-dd>] records an expense. The date is optional and
  defaults to today, as most expenses are recorded on the day.
* expenses lists every recorded expense, numbered.
* delete-expense <number> removes one, e.g. after a typo.

The /amount, /category, and /on flags follow the style of the existing
deadline and event commands, so users only need to learn one style.
Expenses are loaded along with tasks when Rocky starts, so both the
text UI and the GUI get the new commands.

A description containing "|" is rejected, because "|" separates the
fields in the save file and would corrupt the saved line.

With three more commands, getResponse() would grow well beyond 30
lines, so the command dispatch moves into a separate runCommand(),
leaving getResponse() to turn errors into replies.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Add JUnit tests for core logic
commitResults.messageBody:
JUnit is configured in build.gradle, but the project has no tests. A
change to command parsing, date handling, or the save file can break
existing behavior without anyone noticing until the app is used.

Let's add JUnit tests for the highest-value logic, covering 47 of the
65 methods (72%):

* RockyTest: every command via getResponse(), including error replies,
  the save-file format, and loading a save file with malformed lines
* DeadlineTest, EventTest: date parsing and display
* TaskTypeTest: looking up task types by keyword and by icon
* TaskTest, ToDoTest: marking tasks done and how they are displayed

Rocky saves to data/ relative to the working directory, so running the
tests from the project folder would overwrite the user's real task
list. Let's run the Gradle test task in build/test-run/ instead, and
make RockyTest refuse to run from the project folder.

Also, let's add a Testing section to AGENTS.md that sets a ~50% method
coverage target for JUnit tests and requires the tests to be updated
after every code change, so the codebase keeps meeting that target.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Give Rocky his Project Hail Mary voice
commitResults.messageBody:
Rocky's replies use generic chatbot phrases such as "Got it. I've added
this task:", which give him no personality, even though he is named
after the alien engineer from Project Hail Mary.

Let's have each successful command open with a line in Rocky's own
voice, e.g. "Task complete! Good good good. I record success." for
mark, while keeping the details below it (the task or expense, the
updated count, or the numbered list), so no information is lost.

The phrases are named constants, and the three task-adding phrases are
chosen by a switch expression over TaskType, so adding a task type
without a phrase becomes a compile error rather than a missing reply.

Error messages keep their plain wording, because a user who made a
mistake needs a clear explanation of how to fix it more than a themed
reply.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Use a dark Hail Mary theme in the GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
The chat window uses the default light background with pale grey and
green bubbles. It doesn't match Rocky's new Project Hail Mary voice,
and the two sides of the conversation look much alike.

Let's give the window a black, space-like background with a dark input
bar, and show Rocky's replies in amber bubbles, like his rocky shell,
and the user's messages, as Ryland Grace, in blue ones. Both bubble
colors contrast strongly with the black background and with their own
text, so messages stay easy to read.

The styles are inline constants rather than a separate CSS file, as
the theme only changes a handful of properties.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Show profile pictures beside chat bubbles
commitResults.messageBody:
In the chat window, the only way to tell who said what is which side a
bubble sits on, and neither Rocky nor the user has a picture.

Let's show a round profile picture beside every bubble: Rocky's before
his replies on the left, and Ryland Grace's after the user's messages
on the right. The pictures are bundled from src/main/resources/images,
so they are included in the JAR as well.

Each picture is cropped to a square from the top middle of the image,
since a portrait's face is usually near the top, and each image is
loaded once and shared by every dialog box. If an image is missing or
unreadable, a plain circle in the speaker's bubble color is shown
instead, so the chat still works without the pictures.

The bubbles are narrowed slightly to leave room for the pictures.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Shorten and reword Rocky's replies
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot's personality is based on Rocky, the alien engineer from
Andy Weir's novel Project Hail Mary. In the book, Rocky talks with the
human astronaut Ryland Grace through a translation system they build
together, so his English comes out in short, simple sentences with
few extra words, often repeating a word for emphasis. He is also
endlessly practical and loyal, which suits a chatbot whose job is to
keep track of the user's tasks and spending.

The GUI follows the same theme. The chat window has a black,
space-like background; Rocky's replies appear in amber bubbles, like
his rocky shell, and the user's messages appear in blue bubbles, as
Ryland Grace. Each bubble has a round profile picture of its speaker
beside it, so the conversation reads like the two of them talking.

However, several of Rocky's replies are still long, e.g. the deadline
reply "Task with deadline. I track time carefully. Human time units,
difficult, but I manage." Long, elaborate lines don't match Rocky's
clipped way of speaking, and they wrap across several lines in the
GUI's narrow chat bubbles, pushing the details of the task or expense
further down.

Let's shorten or reword seven replies (todo, deadline, list, unmark,
delete, expense, and bye) down to their core message, e.g. "Task
removed. Gone." for delete, so Rocky sounds more like himself and his
replies stay compact. The replies to event, mark, find, expenses, and
delete-expense are unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #4 from d1sha1/branch-A-Personality
commitResults.messageBody: Branch-A-Personality

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Show commands and replies differently
commitResults.messageBody:
The chat window shows both sides of the conversation the same way: a
colored bubble with a round picture, mirrored left and right, as if two
people were chatting. However, the conversation is between a user and
an app: the user types short commands, while Rocky's replies carry the
information the user needs.

Let's show the two sides differently to match. Each command is echoed
as a compact, terminal-style line on the right, in a monospace font
with a "> " prompt. Each reply is a wider amber card beside Rocky's
picture, stretching across the rest of the row.

The user's picture of Ryland Grace is kept but made smaller than
Rocky's, so the user's side stays in the background and the replies
stand out.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Highlight error replies in the GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
When the user types an invalid command, e.g. "todo" without a
description, Rocky's reply explaining the mistake looks the same as any
other reply. It is easy to miss, so the user may not notice that the
command did nothing.

Let's show error replies as a dark red alert card with a bright red
border and a round red "!" badge, instead of an amber card, so a
mistake catches the user's attention at a glance.

To do this, the GUI needs to know which replies are errors, but
getResponse() only returns the reply text. Let's add a Rocky.Reply
record holding the text and whether it is an error, returned by a new
getReply(). getResponse() now delegates to getReply(), so the text UI
works exactly as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Chatbot: Make chat messages adapt to window width
commitResults.messageBody:
The chat window can be resized, but its messages don't adapt well. In a
wide window, Rocky's cards stretch from edge to edge, making lines too
long to read comfortably, while the user's commands stay capped at
300px, so a long command wraps into a narrow block even though there is
plenty of free space beside it.

Let's cap Rocky's cards at a comfortable reading width of 640px, and
let commands wrap at 60% of their row once that is wider than 300px.
The command width is bound to the row's width, so it updates live as
the user resizes the window. In small windows, the layout is unchanged.

commitResults.messageBody:

A-CodeQuality, A-JUnit, D-Expenses and A-BetterGui increments landed.
It restructured the code into packages by splitting Rocky.java into
separate Parser, Storage, Ui and TaskList classes. Master has since
rewritten Rocky.java heavily in place, so a normal merge conflicts in
seven files: a modify/delete on Rocky.java that Git cannot pair with
the five-way split, plus six header clashes where both sides changed
the first line of the file. Resolving those in favour of either side
leaves a tree that does not compile, and the classes extracted on
A-Packages were built against a much older 283-line Rocky that has no
find command, assertions, expenses or GUI support.

Let's merge with the "ours" strategy, which records A-Packages as
merged while keeping master's tree byte for byte. This keeps the
branch history connected without importing a refactoring that no
longer fits, and leaves the packaging to be redone against master's
current Rocky.
